extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of narratology / literary theory; advanced readers and creative writers interested in narrative temporality
extracted.subtask_description: Framework for analyzing 'frequency' in narrative — the relations of repetition between narrative discourse and the diegesis (how many times events are told vs. how many times they occur), including types (singulative, iterative, repeating), subtypes (internal/external/pseudo-iterative) and formal properties (determination, specification, extension, regularity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequency (narrative frequency)
rubrics_metrics.description: What I call narrative frequency, that is, the relations of frequency (or, more simply, of repetition) between the narrative and the diegesis; one of the main aspects of narrative temporality (grammarians call this aspect 'aspect').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat frequency as a primary axis of temporal analysis: an event can happen once or repeatedly, and the narrative may recount it once or several times. Recognize that 'repetition' is a mental abstraction (identity of multiple occurrences is constructed by preserving shared features).

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrating once what happened once (singulative / singular scene) (INIlS)
rubrics_metrics.description: A statement where the singularness of the narrative statement corresponds to the singularness of the narrated event (e.g., 'Yesterday, I went to bed early'). Genette proposes to call this singulative narrative (also 'singular').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the most common narrative form and is treated as the default 'normal' scene; label and identify singulative scenes when analysing narrative temporality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrating n times what happened n times (nN/nS, anaphoric/singulative)
rubrics_metrics.description: A sequence where repeated narrative statements correspond to repeated events (e.g., 'Monday I went to bed early, Tuesday I went to bed early...').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Genette treats this as effectively singulative because of equality of counts: the definition of 'singulative' is the equality of numbers of occurrences on both sides. Note its iconic relation between story-repetition and narrative-repetition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrating n times what happened once (nN/1nS)
rubrics_metrics.description: The narrative tells the same single event several times ('Yesterday I went to bed early, yesterday I went to bed early...' ), i.e., multiple narrative statements about one event.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Occurs in modern texts (repeated episode told differently, or told from different points of view — e.g., Rashomon, The Sound and the Fury), in epistolary contrasts, and in repeating anachronies (advance notices/recalls). It can be stylistic (variations in wording/point of view) or structural (recurrent episode).

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrating one time what happened n times (1N/nS) — Iterative narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: A single narrative utterance takes upon itself several occurrences together (i.e., one statement covers many analogous events). Genette calls this iterative narrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Iterative narration often functions like description or 'moral portrait' and can serve as informative frame/background. In classical narrative it is often subordinate to singulative narration; in Proust it can be dominant and emancipated, providing thematic and rhythmic structuring of large textual passages.

rubrics_metrics.name: External (generalizing) iteration
rubrics_metrics.description: Iterative passages inserted into a singulative scene whose temporal field extends well beyond the temporal field of the enclosing scene (they 'open a window onto the external period').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Label such iterations as generalizing/external; they synthesize occurrences scattered over a longer period than the host scene (e.g., summaries of months/years inside a single scene).

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal (synthesizing) iteration
rubrics_metrics.description: The iterative syllepsis extends over the period of the scene itself and synthesizes repeated micro-occurrences within the scene (e.g., hyperbolic 'every other minute' recurrences).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify passages where duration inside a single scene is treated iteratively (enumeration of classes of occurrences that synthesize diverse events filling the scene). This produces a paradigmatic, classificatory treatment of the scene's events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pseudo-iterative
rubrics_metrics.description: Scenes presented, particularly by their wording in the imperfect, as iterative, while their detail/richness makes it impossible to believe they literally recur; a rhetorical/pseudo-iterative figure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In classical narrative this is usually hyperbolic/figurative (reader understands as sample). In Proust, pseudo-iteration is often inflated toward an impossible literalness; note the author's intent and the reader's 'willing suspension of disbelief.' Examples: recurrently-worded conversations that are actually singular.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iterative contamination of singulative scenes / blending of types
rubrics_metrics.description: A singulative scene can contain iterative passages; the two modes can blend to the point of making temporal demarcation between scene and series indistinct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analysing a scene, watch for internal iterative digressions, external generalizations, or passages that shift between singulative and iterative treatments; such contamination affects rhythm and temporality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regularity / law of recurrence (frequency must be discernible)
rubrics_metrics.description: The repetition that satisfies the spirit is not mere recurrence but recurrence that is regular, obeying a law of frequency that is discernible and formulable — hence predictable in its effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses should look for identifiable rhythms (e.g., 'every Saturday', 'once a week', 'every other day') rather than accidental or purely anecdotal repetition; the discovery of a recurrence law is central to understanding iterative narrative's effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determination, Specification, Extension (three formal properties of an iterative series)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every iterative narrative is a synthetic narrating of events composed of singular units; the series is defined by: determination (diachronic limits: beginning/end), specification (rhythm of recurrence: e.g., every day, sometimes, certain days), and extension (diachronic extent/duration of each unit).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these three axes when defining an iterative series. Determination can be implicit or explicit; specification can be simple/definite/indefinite or complex (superimposed laws); extension controls how much narrative material one unit can yield (pinpointed vs. expandable).

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex specifications / embedding of recurrence laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Two or more laws of recurrence can be superimposed so that iterative units are embedded (e.g., 'every Saturday in May').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize and describe composite recurrence laws when present; this nesting can produce complex rhythmic patterns governing narrative iterations (as in Combray's layered specifications).

rubrics_metrics.name: Extension and the problem of concreteness (avoiding diagrammatic barrenness)
rubrics_metrics.description: If an iterative narrative retains only invariant features common to all units, it reduces to a barren timetable; to 'concretize' the narrative, internal determinations and specifications must be introduced to diversify units.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an iterative unit has sufficient temporal extension (e.g., a Sunday at Combray) the narrator must supply internal variations, particularizations or embedded specifications to create narrative interest and avoid a mere schedule. Analyze how authors concretize iterations (internal determinations) to sustain narrative expansion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repetition as abstraction / problem of identity
rubrics_metrics.description: The identity of repeated events is debatable: repetition is a mental construction that eliminates peculiarities to preserve shared traits ('the sun', 'to rise'); 'identical events' are series of similar events considered in terms of resemblance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating repeated events, account for the abstracting operation: what is treated as 'the same' is a constructed similarity. Use this idea to read how narratives present recurrence (paradigmatic sampling, stereotypes, or claimed literal repetition).
